tagline: Chaparral and spring lupine along a highway that escaped full freeway conversion
intro: Route 68 heads inland from Highway 1 near the Monterey County Fairgrounds, passing Monterey Regional Airport and the junction for Del Rey Oaks. Caltrans designates the section from Highway 1 to the Salinas River as scenic. That 14-mile stretch offers views of chaparral and springtime lupine, the landscape features behind its scenic status. The Monterey-Salinas Highway begins with a freeway section before continuing past the airport toward the inland communities. It is one part of the longer SR 68, which runs from Pacific Grove to Salinas.

In 1937, a dirt wagon road became a paved two-lane highway. Caltrans planned a freeway between Monterey and Salinas during the 1950s and 1960s, but environmental concerns ended that plan. Only short sections were built. The Spreckels section opened in 1967 with two new Salinas River bridges, replacing an 1889 truss bridge. The built eastern segment bypassed Toro Park, leaving a three-mile fragment of the larger scheme.

Driving east from Monterey, the route passes Laguna Seca, then Laureles Grade, Corral de Tierra and San Benancio before Toro Park and Spreckels. The Salinas River marks the end of the designated scenery; the numbered highway continues into Salinas, becoming South Main Street and then following John Street to U.S. 101.

moments.title: Laguna Seca
moments.text: Laguna Seca’s circuit was laid out around a dry lake bed, which gave the track its Spanish name. Local businesses and individuals raised $1.5 million to build it in 1957 on part of the Army’s Fort Ord, after the Pebble Beach Road Races were abandoned as too dangerous. Architect Wallace Holm marked the course in the dirt and walked its line for the bulldozers. The circuit has since changed, but its Corkscrew combines a blind approach with a 59-foot drop. In 1974, the property passed to the Monterey County Parks Department and became part of its park system.

moments.title: Corral de Tierra
moments.text: Castle Rock gave Corral de Tierra its name: a fence of earth. John Steinbeck and his sister Mary played at its base as children. Steinbeck later set The Pastures of Heaven, his 1932 cycle of short stories, in the valley. The community lies along Highway 68 between Salinas and the Monterey Peninsula, on land formerly within Rancho Corral de Tierra. The neighboring San Benancio Canyon also appears in the landscape behind Steinbeck’s stories. Its slopes carry California live oaks, wild sage brush and grass, while Toro Creek runs beside the canyon walls.

moments.title: Spreckels
moments.text: Spreckels was built to house sugar-factory workers. The Spreckels Sugar Company plant operated here from 1899 to 1982, processing beets on an industrial scale. When it opened, it consumed 13 million U.S. gallons of water a day to process 3,000 short tons of beets, with much of that water pumped from wells. The company began selling houses to the public in about 1925, loosening its control of the town. John Steinbeck lived and worked here for a time. The community sits on the north side of the Salinas River, south of Salinas.
